name: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease

ethnicAssociations: Genetic CJD (E200K mutation) more common in Libyan Jews and Slovakian populations
Variant CJD predominantly reported in UK

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: CDC Diagnostic Criteria for Sporadic CJD (Updated 2018)

criteria.description: At least two of: myoclonus, visual/cerebellar signs, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, akinetic mutism
Positive RT-QuIC assay in CSF or other tissues
Typical EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs)
Elevated CSF 14-3-3 protein with clinical duration to death <2 years
MRI DWI/FLAIR showing high signal in caudate/putamen or at least 2 cortical regions

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Probable sCJD: progressive dementia with at least 2 clinical features AND positive RT-QuIC or 1 of (typical EEG, positive 14-3-3, typical MRI). Definite CJD requires neuropathological confirmation.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: RT-QuIC has >95% sensitivity and ~99% specificity, making it the most useful antemortem diagnostic test. Forms include sporadic (85%), genetic (10-15%), and acquired (iatrogenic, variant) CJD.

pathognomonic.notes: Weeks to months course; from normal cognition to severe dementia
Startle myoclonus; may be triggered by noise or touch
Terminal stage; unresponsive but appears awake

common.notes: May be presenting symptom in some subtypes (MV2, VV2)
Anxiety, depression, withdrawal, personality change early in course

occasional.notes: Prominent in fatal familial insomnia variant
Rare; more common in some genetic subtypes

searchTerms: paralysis of up and down gaze

rare.notes: Can mimic ALS in rare presentations

laboratory: CSF RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion): >95% sensitivity and ~99% specificity
CSF 14-3-3 protein elevation (sensitive but not specific)
CSF total tau markedly elevated (typically >1150 pg/mL)
Normal CSF cell count and glucose
imaging: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning (high signal in cortical ribbon pattern)
MRI DWI/FLAIR: high signal in caudate and putamen
MRI: progressive cortical and subcortical atrophy
Variant CJD: pulvinar sign (high signal in posterior thalamus)
genetic: PRNP gene sequencing for genetic/familial forms
PRNP codon 129 polymorphism affects disease phenotype and susceptibility
D178N + codon 129M = fatal familial insomnia; D178N + codon 129V = genetic CJD
other: EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) at 1-2 Hz (more common in later stages and sCJD MM1 subtype)
Neuropathology (definitive diagnosis): spongiform change, neuronal loss, gliosis, PrPSc immunostaining
Prion protein immunohistochemistry or Western blot on brain tissue

distinguishingFeatures: AE may have identifiable antibodies (NMDA-R, LGI1, CASPR2)
AE MRI pattern differs (medial temporal, not cortical ribboning)
Alzheimer's typically progresses over years, not weeks to months
Alzheimer's has amyloid PET positivity and tau biomarker abnormalities
CJD has cortical ribboning on DWI MRI
Hashimoto's MRI is typically less striking
Hashimoto's does not have RT-QuIC positivity

redFlags: CJD is invariably fatal; median survival 5-6 months for sporadic CJD
Rapidly progressive dementia in months demands urgent CJD workup
Treatable mimics (autoimmune encephalitis, infectious encephalitis) must be excluded promptly
Positive RT-QuIC essentially confirms prion disease and should guide goals of care discussions
Special infection control precautions required for surgical instruments and tissue handling
Variant CJD should be considered in younger patients with psychiatric presentation and painful dysesthesias
references: Hermann P, et al. Biomarkers and diagnostic guidelines for sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Lancet Neurol. 2021;20(3):235-246.
Zerr I, et al. Updated clinical diagnostic criteria for sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Brain. 2009;132(Pt 10):2659-2668.
Watson N, et al. The importance of ongoing international surveillance for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Nat Rev Neurol. 2021;17(6):362-379.
